text.p: Wall Street analysts grew more sceptical Thursday about the possibility of America Online Inc. buying rival online computer service CompuServe Corp. while both companies kept silent.

In a separate development, America Online announced it reached a preliminary agreement in a national class-action lawsuit filed against it over recent problems subscribers had connecting to the world's No. 1 online service.
As part of the agreement, America Online will expand refunds and credits to cover subscribers who had difficulty logging on in February and March, the company said.

America Online did not say how much the agreement over the lawsuit would cost. But a spokeswoman said the company believed a $24 million charge it took against second-quarter earnings to pay for a January refund settlement with 36 state attorneys general will cover the expanded refunds and credits.
"We really see that the statement allows us to close the chapter on the access problem," an America Online spokeswoman said.

On the merger front, CompuServe reiterated Wednesday's statement, saying it and its tax preparer parent, H&R Block Inc. were "in external discussions regarding a possible business combination involving CompuServe."

Discussions with America Online, known popularly as AOL, have taken place, and may still be going on, analysts agreed. But several added they viewed a merger of industry leader America Online with No. 2 CompuServe as ill-advised and improbable.
"An AOL-CompuServe deal is highly unlikely. We just don't think it's going to happen. Anyone who suggests it will should check their sources," said investment bank Cowen & Co. analyst Scott Reamer.
"I think (CompuServe) has talked to AOL in the past, but I think there's a lot of other people they could be talking to," said Nesbitt Burns analyst Abhishek Gami.

Whispered by analysts as additional possible CompuServe suitors were AT&T Corp., Microsoft Corp., MCI Communications Corp., Sprint Corp., British Telecommunications Plc and the Baby Bells, as well as former CompuServe managers joined in a venture capital firm.

The giants may be wary of online services due to the problems that International Business Machines Corp. and Sears Roebuck and Co. had with the Prodigy service before selling it last year, said Widmann Siff analyst Ernest Widmann.

But analysts also said larger players would be much better placed than America Online to pay cash for CompuServe, which is 80 percent owned by Kansas City, Mo.-based Block and could fetch as much as $2 billion.
"Microsoft and AT&T could pay more," said investment bank Brean Murray analyst Barbara Chacour.
Still, Block has been trying so long to break away from CompuServe that it might bite at an America Online offer, analysts said.
America Online's balance sheet would not easily permit a cash deal. "I suppose there's some way an investment banking firm might structure something," said brokerage Dean Witter analyst Paul Mackey.
More likely, however, would be an offer comprised largely of America Online stock. "If Block took stock in AOL, it would only make their situation worse, not better," Mackey said.
An America Online spokesman declined to comment. Block repeated CompuServe's statement.
America Online stock rose 87.5 cents to $45.50 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange, while CompuServe edged up 12.5 cents to $12.75 on Nasdaq.
Even if a deal could be done, analysts questioned its wisdom and workability. "It would be a tough merger because these companies have hated each other," Chacour said.
A CompuServe acquisition would add about 3.1 million U.S. and European subscribers to America Online's existing base of eight million members.
